chapter.name: Keeping Time with the Skies
chapter.blurb: How the Moon's changing appearance through the month is caused by how much of its sunlit half faces the Earth as it revolves; how the natural cycles of the day, the month and the year, measured from the Sun's highest position, the Moon's phases and the Earth's revolution, gave rise to lunar, solar and luni-solar calendars including the Indian National Calendar; why many Indian festivals shift on the Gregorian calendar while a few stay almost fixed; and why countries launch artificial satellites alongside Earth's own natural satellite, the Moon.

scope_in.item: Why the Moon's appearance changes: illumination geometry, positions A-H, gibbous/crescent/full/new Moon, waxing/waning, Shukla/Krishna Paksha, and why this is not caused by the Earth's shadow

Locating the Moon in the sky: moonrise about 50 minutes later each day and why, waxing Moon at sunset/waning Moon at sunrise, New Moon closest to and Full Moon farthest from the Sun in the sky, and when lunar and solar eclipses can occur
Natural periodic units of time: the mean solar day (about 24 hours, found from the Sun's highest position/shortest shadow), the lunar month (about 29.5 days), and the solar year (about 365.25 days)

Lunar calendars, solar calendars (including the Gregorian leap year rule and its 100/400-year refinement, and the tropical vs sidereal year), luni-solar calendars (Adhika Maasa, Amant and Purnimant calendars, Indian month names), and the Indian National Calendar including the Calendar Reform Committee

Festivals tied to lunar/luni-solar calendars (Diwali, Holi, Buddha Purnima, Eid-ul-Fitr, Dussehra) and their shifting Gregorian dates; festivals tied to a solar sidereal calendar (Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Bihu, Vaisakhi, Poila Baisakh, Puthandu) and their near-fixed dates; solstices, equinoxes, Uttarayan and Dakshinayan; the Rashtriya Panchang

The Moon as Earth's natural satellite and artificial satellites: typical orbit height and period, their uses, named ISRO missions (Cartosat, Bhuvan, AstroSat, Chandrayaan, Aditya L1, Mangalyaan, student satellites), and space debris

concepts.name: Phases of the Moon: why the Moon's appearance changes
concepts.description: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight, and only the illuminated half facing the Sun receives light; the changing portion of this illuminated half that faces the Earth as the Moon revolves around it produces the phases of the Moon.
concepts.idea: The Moon does not make its own light. Its phases are caused by how much of its sunlit half faces the Earth at different points in its monthly revolution, not by the Earth's shadow.
concepts.rule: The Moon does not emit light of its own; it shines because it reflects sunlight that falls on it. The half of the Moon that faces the Sun is illuminated, and the other half, facing away from the Sun, is non-illuminated. The Moon revolves around the Earth, and only one half of it always faces the Earth, but the portion facing the Earth is not always the illuminated portion. We can only see the illuminated part of the Moon that faces the Earth. In a ball-and-torch activity, a small ball on a stick represents the Moon, a torch or lamp represents the Sun, and a person's head represents the Earth. When the ball is held opposite the lamp, the entire illuminated portion faces the observer, just like the full Moon (Purnima). When the ball is held towards the lamp, the non-illuminated portion faces the observer, just like the new Moon (Amavasya), and no illuminated portion can be seen at all. At in-between positions, the line separating the illuminated and non-illuminated portions appears curved. Using eight positions labelled A to H around the Earth, position A (opposite the Sun) gives the full Moon, and position E (towards the Sun) gives the new Moon. At positions B and H, more than half of the illuminated portion is seen, called the gibbous phase; at positions D and F, less than half is seen, called the crescent phase. The changing shapes of the bright portion of the Moon from one day to another, as seen from Earth, are called the phases of the Moon. The bright portion shrinks from full to new over about two weeks, called the waning period or Krishna Paksha in India, and then grows from new back to full over about two weeks, called the waxing period or Shukla Paksha. The full cycle from one full Moon to the next takes about a month. A common but incorrect explanation is that the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon causes its phases; this is wrong, since the Earth's shadow on the Moon only causes a lunar eclipse, a separate and much rarer event, and phases occur every month because of the changing relative positions of the Sun, Moon and Earth.
concepts.example: When the Moon is at the position directly opposite the Sun as seen from Earth, the entire illuminated half faces the Earth, and we see a full Moon.

concepts.name: Locating the Moon: moonrise timing and eclipses
concepts.description: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day because it moves ahead in its orbit while the Earth rotates once every 24 hours; this same changing position explains when a lunar or a solar eclipse can and cannot occur.
concepts.idea: Where and when the Moon can be seen in the sky changes every day in a predictable way, and this same idea of relative position explains why eclipses only happen on certain Moon phases, and not every month.
concepts.rule: On a full Moon day, the Moon is nearly opposite the Sun: when the Sun rises in the East, the Moon is almost setting in the West. On successive mornings at sunrise, as its bright part continues to decrease, the Moon appears to move closer in the sky to the Sun; when the bright part decreases to a half circle, the Moon is overhead at sunrise. A waxing Moon is easiest to spot at sunset, and a waning Moon is easiest to spot at sunrise; because of these shifts, the Moon always rises and sets at different times than the Sun. The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day; sometimes moonrise happens in the afternoon, around 2 to 4 p.m., so the Moon can be seen in the eastern sky during daylight, and it can take about 30 minutes past the listed moonrise time for the Moon to climb high enough to be seen. This delay happens because the Moon moves ahead a little in its orbit around the Earth in the time the Earth completes one rotation in 24 hours, so the Earth needs to rotate a little more for the Moon to appear in nearly the same spot in the sky. On the New Moon day, the Moon appears closest to the Sun in the sky, and it appears farthest from the Sun on the Full Moon day. The Moon's phases are not caused by the Earth's shadow falling on it; that incorrect idea is a common misconception. Instead, a lunar eclipse can only happen on a full Moon day, when the Earth can come between the Sun and the Moon, and a solar eclipse can only happen on a new Moon day, when the Moon can come between the Earth and the Sun. Eclipses do not occur every month, because of the small tilt of the Moon's orbit with respect to the Earth's orbit around the Sun, which usually keeps the three bodies from lining up exactly.
concepts.example: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day than the day before, because it has moved ahead a little in its orbit around the Earth.

concepts.name: Measuring time: the day, month and year as natural periodic units
concepts.description: The day, the month and the year are each based on a different natural periodic cycle: the Earth's rotation, the Moon's phase cycle, and the Earth's revolution around the Sun.
concepts.idea: Three different repeating cycles in the sky give us the day, the month and the year, and each can be measured by careful observation, such as timing a shadow or counting Moon phases.
concepts.rule: When viewed from the Earth, the Sun appears to rise in the East, set in the West, and rise again the next day; this apparent periodic motion is primarily due to the rotation of the Earth around its own axis, and this natural cycle is the foundation of the day, a unit to measure time. The average time the Sun takes to go from its highest position in the sky on one day to its highest position the next day is 24 hours, and is called the mean solar day. The highest position of the Sun can be found by measuring the length of the shadow cast by a vertical object; the shadow is shortest when the Sun is at its highest point. By marking the tip of a stick's shadow at intervals and finding when the shadow is shortest on successive days, the duration of a solar day can be measured, and it comes out close to 24 hours. The phases of the Moon give another natural cycle: the Moon takes about 29.5 days, nearly a month, to cycle through all its phases, and this cycle is the basis for the month. The next larger unit of time is related to the cycle of seasons: the Earth revolves around the Sun and takes nearly 365 and a quarter days to complete one revolution, undergoing one cycle of seasons in that time, which defines the solar year.
concepts.example: Marking when a stick's shadow is shortest on two consecutive days and finding the time difference gives an estimate of the mean solar day, close to 24 hours.

concepts.name: Lunar, solar and luni-solar calendars, and the Indian National Calendar
concepts.description: Lunar calendars track the Moon's phases but drift from the seasons; solar calendars like the Gregorian calendar stay synced to the seasons using a leap year rule; luni-solar calendars combine both by adding an intercalary month; the Indian National Calendar is a solar calendar built on traditional month names.
concepts.idea: Different calendars solve the same problem, keeping track of time, in different ways: by following the Moon alone, the Sun alone, or a combination of the two, corrected periodically to stay accurate.
concepts.rule: In a lunar calendar, the day is the shortest unit, a month is nearly 29.5 days, and a lunar year of 12 lunar months is about 354 days; the phases of the Moon give an easy way to track time, but since the seasons repeat in approximately 365 days, the seasons do not remain synchronised to the same lunar months in successive lunar years. Solar calendars, needed to know the arrival of seasons for agriculture, keep the year synced to the seasons; the Gregorian calendar, widely used today, is a solar calendar whose months are adjusted to add up to 365 days, with some months having 30 days, others 31, and February 28. Since the Earth takes nearly an extra quarter day beyond 365 days to go around the Sun, these extra hours add up to about one day every four years, so solar calendars add a leap day (29 February) every four years; over longer periods, leap years are skipped every 100 years, such as 1700, 1800 and 1900, but added back every 400 years, such as 1600 and 2000, to stay accurately matched to the seasons. The time between successive spring equinoxes is called the tropical year, and the Gregorian calendar is based on the tropical year; the time for the same stars to rise again at sunset is called the sidereal year, which is longer than the tropical year by about 20 minutes and is used by astronomers. A luni-solar calendar primarily uses the Moon's phases for counting days and months, but makes adjustments to stay in sync with the cycle of seasons; since 12 lunar months add up to 354 days, about 11 days short of the solar year, every 2-3 years an extra month, called Adhika Maasa or the intercalary month, is added. Indian luni-solar month names include Chaitra, Vaisakha, Jyeshtha, Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada, Ashwin, Kartika, Margashirsha, Pausha, Magha and Phalguna; in Amant calendars, the new month starts the day after the new Moon and ends on the new Moon, while in Purnimant calendars, the new month starts the day after the full Moon and ends on the full Moon. The Indian National Calendar, used alongside the Gregorian calendar for official purposes, is a solar calendar of 365 days that begins on 22 March, the day after the spring equinox; its months have either 30 or 31 days, with the second to sixth months having 31 days and the rest 30, and leap years are matched to the Gregorian calendar by adding a day to Chaitra, the first month, so in leap years the new year begins on 21 March. In 1952, the Government of India set up a Calendar Reform Committee, which recommended the Unified National Calendar, adopted from 21 March 1956 CE, that is, 1 Chaitra 1878 Saka; the Indian National Calendar follows the general principles of the Surya Siddhanta.

concepts.name: Festivals and astronomical cycles
concepts.description: Many Indian festivals are tied to the Moon's phases through lunar or luni-solar calendars, so their Gregorian dates shift each year, while a few festivals tied to the solstices follow a solar sidereal calendar and stay almost fixed on the Gregorian calendar.
concepts.idea: Whether a festival's date drifts a little, drifts a lot, or barely drifts at all on the Gregorian calendar depends on whether it follows a luni-solar, a purely lunar, or a solar sidereal calendar.
concepts.rule: Many Indian festivals are tied to the phases of the Moon and are based on either lunar or luni-solar calendars: Diwali falls on the new Moon of Kartika, Holi on the full Moon of Phalguna, Buddha Purnima on the full Moon of Vaisakha, Eid-ul-Fitr after sighting the crescent Moon at the end of Ramazan, and Dussehra on the tenth day of Ashwina; hence they occur on different dates in the Gregorian calendar in successive years. For festivals based on luni-solar calendars, the Gregorian dates shift, but by typically less than a month, because the luni-solar calendar's intercalary month corrects for the difference between the lunar and solar years; purely lunar calendars, with no such correction, drift much further, so a festival like Eid-ul-Fitr can occur in different months of the Gregorian year, moving earlier by about 11 days each year. A few festivals, such as Makar Sankranti, Pongal, Bihu, Vaisakhi, Poila Baisakh and Puthandu, follow a solar sidereal calendar and happen on almost the same Gregorian date every year, since the Gregorian calendar is based on the tropical year, which is very close in length to the sidereal year these festivals follow. Long ago, these festivals were tied to a solstice or an equinox (the Sun's apparent northward movement from December to June is called Uttarayan, and its southward movement from June to December is Dakshinayan, with the extremes around 21 June and 21 December, while on the equinoxes the Sun rises exactly in the East). Because of the small difference between the sidereal and tropical years, and the slow wobble of the Earth's axis, the dates of these sidereal-based festivals slowly shift ahead relative to the solstices and equinoxes over long periods; for example, Makar Sankranti moves ahead by about one day every 71 years. Since the dates of many festivals are based on the exact lunar phase at sunrise, and sunrise occurs earlier in Eastern India than in Western India, these dates can also shift by a day between regions even in the same year; to maintain uniformity, the Positional Astronomy Centre of the Government of India annually publishes the Rashtriya Panchang, a detailed calculation of the positions of celestial objects for a central location in India, giving advance intimation of festival dates for holiday declaration.

concepts.name: Artificial satellites: the Moon as a natural satellite and ISRO's missions
concepts.description: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, while artificial satellites are man-made objects launched into orbit for purposes like communication, navigation and Earth observation; ISRO runs several such missions, and old satellites can become dangerous space debris.
concepts.idea: Just as the Moon naturally orbits the Earth, countries launch man-made satellites into orbit to serve specific purposes, and India's space agency ISRO runs several kinds of these missions.
concepts.rule: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite, orbiting our planet; besides the Moon, man-made satellites sent by various countries also orbit the Earth, appearing as tiny specks moving in the night sky. Most artificial satellites orbit about 800 km above Earth's surface and take roughly 100 minutes to complete one orbit. These satellites help in many ways, including communication, navigation, weather monitoring, disaster management and scientific research; the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) has launched many satellites supporting these activities. The Cartosat series of satellites captures high-quality images of the Earth to improve maps, plan cities, and handle natural disasters in India; a mapping platform called Bhuvan uses these images to show terrain, soil, land use and vegetation. AstroSat, another ISRO mission, makes scientific observations of stars and other celestial objects. India's other space missions include Chandrayaan 1, 2 and 3 to the Moon, Aditya L1 to study the Sun, and Mangalyaan to Mars; ISRO also lets Indian students build and launch small satellites, such as AzaadiSat, InspireSat-1 and Jugnu. A lot of artificial satellites are sent into space by many countries, and after their useful life, many of them and their rocket parts become space junk or space debris, which crowds space and could collide with working satellites; while small debris burns up in the atmosphere as it falls towards the Earth, larger pieces can crash on the ground, so countries are now working together to remove this dangerous debris.
